This underscores the importance of emphasizing the true purpose of your classroom management plan, which is to protect your students’ right to learn and enjoy school.
The “my way or the highway” approach misunderstands the call to be consistent with sternness, strictness, and authoritarianism.
Consistency just means that you’ll do what you say you’ll do—in this case, follow a set of guidelines that protect your students’ freedom to listen, learn, and love school.
It’s not a means of revenge or a way to express your anger. It’s simply a way to ensure a learning environment that is best for them and their education.

t: How To Handle Misbehavior Outside Of Your Classroom -classroom/
q: It’s a thorny issue, because you can’t very well send your students to time-out.
Because as soon as your students learn that they can misbehave away from the classroom without consequence, the floodgates will open.
The first step is to teach your students that class rules apply wherever you are and that they’ll be enforced just the same.
As soon as you leave your classroom, it’s important to stay in position to observe closely and make sure your students are behaving to your expectations.
If you’re going to be away from class for a period of time, like an assembly, then it’s smart to bring along a notebook for documentation.
Students tend to misbehave away from the classroom when they’re unsure whether the class rules still apply.
They’ll behave no different than when they’re in the classroom.
